summary: A white paper from INFN stressing the key points to consider for an IPng plan. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This white paper presents the Italian National Institute for Nuclear Physics network team's requirements for IPng. It asks for a coordinated solution to address and routing problems and a transition that does not disrupt applications or connectivity.

questions: which problems did infn want ipng to solve
subtitle: INFN's proposed requirements for an IPng plan and transition.

tldr.problem: The authors identify address exhaustion, flat address space, and routing efficiency, flexibility, and capacity as problems for IPng to address together.
tldr.mechanism: They propose transparent application migration, flexible addressing and routing, continued datagram service, and a distributed transition that preserves IPv4 connectivity.
tldr.outcome: The memo offers INFN's network experience and says publication does not imply acceptance of its ideas by the IPng area.

today: RFC 1676 is Informational and records INFN's proposed IPng requirements. Its publication does not imply that the IPng area accepted the ideas.

sections.title: Problems IPng Should Address
sections.content:
The INFN network team submitted this white paper in response to the IPng solicitation. It identifies three main problems: address exhaustion, flat address space, and routing efficiency, flexibility, and capacity.

The authors argue that the IPng plan should solve these problems together. They also call for transparency to end users and flexibility as communication technology and network topology change.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors want IPng to address address shortages and routing limits as a connected problem. Users' applications should not be affected by the transition.

sections.title: Transport, Addressing, and Routing
sections.content:
The memo says TCP should keep the same interfaces and services for applications, while applications should be able to use other transport services through a transport selector. The network layer should continue to provide a datagram service. It describes CLNS and its 20-byte NSAP address as a possible starting point, noting its hierarchical format and existing operational experience.

The authors say routing protocols can change without affecting end-system configuration, but address aggregation, hierarchical topology, and policy-based routing matter. They also call for multicast and leave lower-layer media open to future evolution. They do not consider source routing a major issue.
sections.plainLanguage: Applications should keep their existing TCP interface, while IPng could offer other transport choices. The authors favor flexible hierarchical addresses and policy-based routing.

sections.title: Transition and Deployment
sections.content:
Based on their experience moving a DECnet network to DECnet/OSI over CLNS, the authors recommend distributed transition planning. Each organization should be able to plan and begin migration without losing connectivity, and new systems should interwork with both IPv4 and IPng using the same applications.

The memo favors dual stack over translation as a simpler transition method, but says backward compatibility needs a defined deadline. It notes that dual stack continues IPv4 address exhaustion and requires continued support for IPv4 routing; the authors expect a goal of global IPng connectivity once no IPv4-only hosts remain.
sections.plainLanguage: Organizations should be able to transition at their own pace while keeping connectivity. The memo favors dual stack but warns that IPv4 support needs a defined end point.

sections.title: Status of the White Paper
sections.content: RFC 1676 is an informational submission to the IETF IPng area. It states that publication does not imply acceptance of any idea expressed in the document.
sections.plainLanguage: This document presents INFN's views for IPng discussions. It does not establish a standard or show that its ideas were accepted.

references.text: Gross, P., ed., "IP: Next Generation (IPng) White Paper Solicitation", RFC 1550, December 1993.
